summary: Defines a DHCP option used to configure devices deployed within CableLabs architectures. It specifically describes content for a PacketCable Media Terminal Adapter and is meant to be extended as other CableLabs client devices appear.

plainLanguage.summary: Cable companies need to set up devices at customers' homes automatically. This defines an extra DHCP setting to tell those cable phone adapters what to do.

questions: what is the cablelabs client configuration option
subtitle: A DHCP option that tells cable voice adapters which servers, realm and timers to use when they start up.

tldr.problem: PacketCable voice adapters (MTAs) and their cable modems may be run by different companies, and the MTA needs special settings such as server addresses and a Kerberos realm that ordinary DHCP options do not carry.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3495 defines DHCP option 122, the CableLabs Client Configuration (CCC) option, which holds numbered sub-options for DHCP servers, the provisioning server, Kerberos retry timers, the realm name, ticket use and a provisioning timer.
tldr.outcome: The option is a Proposed Standard with a sub-option number space kept by IANA, so other CableLabs devices can add sub-options later.

today: RFC 3495 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2003, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a CableLabs Option Is Needed
sections.content:
CableLabs is a non-profit consortium that specifies broadband architectures for the cable industry. Its PacketCable project covers Voice over IP, supported at the customer site by a Cable Modem (CM) and a Media Terminal Adapter (MTA). The MTA turns VoIP protocols into analog telephony for an ordinary phone.

The CM and MTA are separate IP devices. Each has its own MAC address and IP configuration and each uses DHCP. The RFC assumes they may be administered by different business entities: the CM is configured by the Data Access Provider's DHCP servers, and the MTA by the Telephony Service Provider's (TSP's) DHCP servers.

Because of the MTA's special configuration needs, a new CableLabs Client Configuration (CCC) option is defined. Both CM and MTA request it, and both the DAP and TSP servers fill it in. The RFC adds that the option will also support non-VoIP uses, so using it does not mean the provider is a TSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Your cable box and your phone adapter can be looked after by different companies. Each needs its own instructions, so a new kind of note is added to the DHCP message.

sections.title: The CCC Option and Sub-Option Format
sections.content:
The option starts with a tag octet holding the option code, 122, then a length octet, then the sub-options. The length does not count the tag or length octets themselves, and it is the total length in octets, not the number of sub-options. If the total exceeds 255 octets, the long-option procedure in RFC 3396 MUST be used to split it into several smaller options.

Each sub-option has the same shape: a sub-option code, a length octet and that many octets of information. Sub-option codes 1 to 8 are defined, and 9 to 255 are reserved for future extensions. Codes 1 and 2 are sent to the cable modem; codes 3 to 8 are sent to the MTA.

Three general encoding rules apply. Domain names MUST be encoded as in RFC 1035 section 3.1, with a terminating 0, and name compression MUST NOT be used. IPv4 addresses are 4 octets in network byte order. All multi-octet quantities use network byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: Each instruction is a little labelled box: a number saying what kind it is, a size, and then the contents. Many boxes sit inside one bigger box.

sections.title: The Eight Sub-Options
sections.content:
Sub-options 1 and 2 give the TSP's primary and secondary DHCP server addresses, the servers from which an MTA is permitted to accept a DHCP OFFER. Length MUST be 4, followed by an IPv4 address.

Sub-option 3 gives the TSP's provisioning server, as either an IPv4 address or an FQDN. A type octet comes first: 1 means IPv4 (length 5) and 0 means FQDN (length n+1).

Sub-options 4 and 5 configure the backoff and retry behaviour of the MTA's Kerberos AS-REQ/AS-REP and AP-REQ/AP-REP exchanges, which RFC 1510 does not define. Each has length 12: a nominal timeout, a maximum timeout and a maximum retry count, each a 32-bit unsigned value. For AS-REQ the nominal timeout is in milliseconds; for AP-REQ it is in seconds. Both maximum timeouts are in seconds.

Sub-option 6 carries the Kerberos realm name, in all capital letters, so the MTA can use DNS to find the TSP's Key Distribution Center. Sub-option 7 is a one-octet boolean (0 or 1) saying whether the MTA should use a Ticket Granting Ticket when getting service tickets. Sub-option 8 is the provisioning timer, one octet from 0 to 255 minutes. If it expires before provisioning completes, the MTA should reset it and restart provisioning from the beginning. A value of 0 means the timer MUST be disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: The eight boxes tell the phone adapter which servers to talk to, how long to wait and how many times to retry, which login realm to use, and how long it may take to get set up.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Use the Option
sections.content:
CableLabs client devices send DHCP requests that include option 55 (Parameter Request List) and option 60 (Vendor Class Identifier). Option 55 asks the server for the CCC option. Option 60 names the device type, which tells the server which CCC sub-options to fill in. The exact sub-options for each device type are set in CableLabs project specifications, such as the PacketCable provisioning specification.

Client devices never put the CCC option in their own DHCP requests. Only servers populate it.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks for the instruction note and says what kind of gadget it is. The server then writes the right instructions for that gadget.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and Legacy Use
sections.content:
IANA assigned option code 122. Before that, the CCC option used the site-specific option value 177 (0xB1), and that use is to be deprecated now that an official number exists.

IANA is also asked to maintain a new number space, CableLabs Client Configuration Sub-options, in the BOOTP-DHCP Parameters registry. New sub-option codes are registered under the IETF Consensus policy of RFC 2434. No registry is needed for the provisioning-server type codes (IPv4 and FQDN) because no more are expected.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number for this note was reserved so nobody else uses it. A list of sub-box numbers is kept so new ones can be added in an orderly way.

sections.title: Misdirection Risks and Mitigations
sections.content:
The CCC option can steer a device to the wrong place by giving it incorrect DHCP server addresses, provisioning server addresses or Kerberos realm names. The RFC lists three threats: a denial of service from invalid addresses, a man-in-the-middle attack by pointing at a snooper, and a malicious TSP stealing customers by changing the realm.

It lists mitigations. The CMTS (head-end) is configured with specific DHCP servers and a correctly configured CMTS only allows downstream traffic from specific IP addresses or ranges. A device that reaches a KDC must still present valid certificates, though the cost of validating them could itself be a DoS opportunity. A TSP found redirecting customers is treated as an administrative matter between the access provider and the TSP. The RFC also points to the DHCP specification and DHCP authentication (RFC 3118).
sections.plainLanguage: If someone gave the phone adapter wrong directions, it could get lost or end up talking to the wrong company. The cable network has several locks to make that hard.

items.label: Primary DHCP server
items.desc: TSP's primary DHCP server address, sent to the CM.

items.label: Secondary DHCP server
items.desc: TSP's secondary DHCP server address, sent to the CM.

items.label: Provisioning server
items.desc: IPv4 address or FQDN, sent to the MTA.

items.label: AS-REQ/AS-REP backoff
items.desc: Timeout and retry values for Kerberos AS exchange.

items.label: AP-REQ/AP-REP backoff
items.desc: Timeout and retry values for Kerberos AP exchange.

items.label: Kerberos realm
items.desc: Realm name used to find the KDC.

items.label: TGS utilization
items.desc: Boolean: whether to use a TGT for service tickets.
